analysis.one_liner: Lets gun-violence victims sue gun makers and dealers by repealing their liability shield.
analysis.headline: The bill to let gun-violence victims sue the gun industry was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, a 2005 law that shields gun and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and their trade associations from most civil lawsuits over the criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm. Repealing it would let shooting victims and their families sue the gun industry in court, like victims of other dangerous products can. The bill died in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Gun violence victims and their families, who would regain the right to sue gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations when negligent sales or marketing contribute to a shooting. Today the 2005 liability shield blocks most of those suits before they can even be heard; the bill would put the gun industry under the same court accountability rules that apply to car makers, drug companies, and other product manufacturers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of gun violence and their families

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which currently prohibits civil actions against firearm or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, or trade associations for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm [S2].

Would restore victims' access to the courts: by striking sections 2, 3, and 4 of the act (15 U.S.C. 7901-7903), the bill removes the legal bar that stops most negligence lawsuits against the gun industry before trial [S3].

Supporters included 15 senators — 14 Democrats and 1 independent — who signed on as cosponsors, arguing victims of gun violence deserve the same day in court as victims of other defective products [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, importers, and their trade associations, which would face negligence lawsuits and litigation costs they are currently immune from. Some of that cost would likely be passed to buyers through higher prices and insurance, and small dealers could face suits over crimes committed with guns they lawfully sold.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and their insurers

drawbacks.text: Repealing the shield would expose law-abiding dealers and manufacturers to lawsuits over third-party crimes committed with products that were legally made and sold — a burden no other legal industry carries, and one that could drive up prices and insurance costs or push small dealers out of business [S2].

The bill was a flat repeal with no carve-outs or alternative standard, so it offered no middle path — such as liability only for negligent sales or marketing — and its single-approach design gave wavering senators nothing to support [S3].

Even with repeal, plaintiffs would still have to prove the industry actor was actually negligent; suits would take years and cost millions, and most would not produce the accountability or compensation victims hope for.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and significant: victims would get the same right to hold a negligent industry accountable in court that they have against makers of cars, drugs, or other consumer products [S2]. The costs fall on a concentrated industry — litigation exposure, insurance, and possibly higher prices — and honest supporters would concede that some suits would target sellers who broke no law at the time of sale. The deeper problem is not the design but the fate of the bill: with no Republican support and no committee action, its benefits were never even debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal and 12 Senate colleagues introduced the bill on June 11, 2019; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary that same day [S5].
The bill would repeal sections 2, 3, and 4 of the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, the law that blocks most civil suits against the gun industry over criminal misuse of firearms [S2].
Fifteen senators — 14 Democrats and 1 independent — cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no companion movement before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations are better off: the 2005 liability shield that protects them from most negligence lawsuits over gun crimes remains fully in place, unchallenged by any hearing or vote. Gun violence victims and their families gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers kept their liability shield

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the effort to repeal the gun industry's liability shield.

for.name: 15 Senate cosponsors (14 Democrats, 1 independent)
for.role: Cosponsors, including Chris Murphy, Dianne Feinstein, and Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican joined.

against.name: Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: His committee never held a hearing or markup on the bill; it stayed in committee with no action after referral.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; as floor manager he controlled which bills got votes.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Long championed and defended the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act the bill sought to repeal, and pressed Republicans to protect it.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independent; not a single Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired Judiciary Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would strip away the 2005 law that shields them from most civil suits over criminal misuse of their products, exposing them to negligence lawsuits and litigation costs for the first time since 2005. Because the bill died, that shield remains intact.

industries.industry: Gun dealers, importers, and trade associations
industries.note: The same liability shield covers sellers, importers, and industry trade groups; repeal would let victims sue them over negligent sales and marketing as well. Their interest in keeping the shield runs directly against victims' access to the courts.

Repeal would raise legal exposure and insurance costs for small, law-abiding dealers, though suits would still require proving negligence. Honest supporters of the bill would acknowledge this spillover cost.
